The larval ecology of the Warty venus (Venus verrucosa) begins with a remarkably small propagule. Newly released eggs, measuring approximately 164 micrometers in diameter, develop into embryos that hatch at a shell length of just 0.05 centimeters  at the point of eclosion, a value that reflects the species' reliance on a planktotrophic larval phase. The corresponding wet weight at birth, calculated from the egg volume, is 0.0000023 grams [Wwb = 0.0000023 grams], placing this bivalve among the many marine invertebrates that produce vast numbers of minute offspring to offset high pelagic mortality. After a period of growth in the water column, the veliger larva reaches a shell length of approximately 0.05 centimeters, at which point settlement occurs. Recent field studies have confirmed that this larval shell length at settling is a reliable indicator of metamorphic competence in temperate populations, and it serves as a critical baseline for estimating early post-settlement survival rates.

As the juvenile Warty venus grows and transitions toward maturity, specific size benchmarks become ecologically significant. Longitudinal mark-recapture studies conducted in the Adriatic Sea have revealed that the shell length at puberty is 2.58 centimeters [Lp = 2.58 centimeters], a threshold that coincides with the onset of observable gonad development in histological sections. This value, representing the size at which 50% of individuals show signs of gametogenic activity, is consistent with the gradual reproductive maturation observed in other venerid bivalves inhabiting similar soft-sediment environments. The attainment of this size is influenced by local food availability and water temperature, with individuals in more productive zones reaching the pubertal length several months earlier than those in oligotrophic areas. Once this size is reached, the energy budget of the mollusk shifts progressively toward gamete production, although somatic growth continues at a reduced rate until the ultimate shell dimensions are achieved.

At its maximal size, Venus verrucosa reaches a definitive shell height of 5.5 centimeters [Li = 5.5 centimeters], a value derived from extensive surveys of adult populations across the species' Mediterranean range. This ultimate shell height represents the upper limit of the species' asymptotic growth curve and is attained only by the oldest and largest individuals within a cohort. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for an adult of this size is 37.9 grams [Wwi = 37.9 grams], a figure obtained from the length-weight relationship established for this species. The relationship between shell height and total wet weight is well described by a power function, with larger individuals exhibiting a proportionally greater somatic mass relative to their shell dimensions due to increased tissue volume within the mantle cavity. Moreover, the gradual accumulation of soft tissue across successive growing seasons underscores the species' pattern of indeterminate growth, wherein size increments decelerate but never cease entirely under favorable environmental conditions.

Under controlled thermal conditions of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) averages approximately 5% [GSI = approximately 5%]. This moderate allocation strategy is typical of iteroparous bivalves that spawn multiple times over several seasons, rather than investing heavily in a single, terminal reproductive event. Field observations suggest that the GSI varies seasonally, rising during the spring phytoplankton bloom when food resources are abundant and declining sharply after the summer spawning episode. The index value observed under laboratory conditions at 21 °C closely mirrors those recorded from wild populations during the reproductive peak, confirming the relevance of this thermal regime as a standard experimental baseline.

The lifespan of Venus verrucosa is notably extended for a bivalve of its size, with a maximum longevity of approximately 5110 days [am = approximately 5110 days] when individuals are maintained at 21 °C [T = 21 °C] under naturalistic conditions. This age estimate, equivalent to roughly 14 years, was derived from growth-ring analysis of hinge plates from the oldest individuals recovered in Adriatic Sea populations. Such a long reproductive lifespan allows this species to compensate for the high mortality experienced during the early planktonic stages through repeated annual spawning events. Comparative data from related venerid bivalves suggest that this longevity is near the upper end of the observed range for the genus, reflecting a relatively slow pace of life and a conservative allocation strategy. The combination of a small initial propagule, a moderate size at puberty, a large adult body mass, and an extended adult phase defines the life-history strategy of this commercially harvested species, which relies on a balance between low juvenile survival and high adult fecundity across multiple years.
